Sounds like better guidance needed. You have to always keep in mind that the agent doesn't understand the repo from the "business" perspective, only from the functional. Whenever I plan epics with an agent I always check on acceptance criteria before the tickets hit the tracker, so I know it gets the business aspect. Tends to lead to far better code.

Yes, it adds tests and makes them pass. But it adds tests for things that no human would ever add. I regularly wind up removing tests where it is guarding dumb crap like "facts" in markdown files, or "drift" across files. Today I came across a file where it was walking ASTs across multiple languages to ensure that there was no drift. I get why it'd do that, but simple changes become absurd.

That's not my experience. Agent usually follows the pattern correctly by creating a relevant test and then making it pass. Where strange tests are more likely to fall in is when agent writes the test after the testee.

> pre-AI

I'd say pre-LLM, just because I don't want to surrender the term "AI" to one particular subtype without a fight.

Some of those complex tools would be "Good Old-Fashioned AI", which generally means stuff doing symbolic logic rather than mystery-weights.

The last point is one I make often. AI cannot be trusted to be deterministic, but they can produce deterministic tools that are verifiable as such.  Those tools I can trust as much as any other complex tool from the pre-AI era.

> Ironically, despite the predictions that AI will murder SaaS, I think the result is they end up even more entrenched, because Job Bob's Bait Shack And Tax Filing Services

OK, so this is slightly different since it's more about how runtime behavior than design-time behavior, but... I'm in a SaaS workplace, and I've been trying to seed the following idea:

1. The very cheapest/fastest end of the market will be eaten up by Job Bob's Bait Shack stuff. Cheap wrappers around a prompt that goes "Pretend you're a computer that obeys the following rules" jank. A race to the bottom we can't win.

2. Most of our (desirable) customers will (eventually) realize they can't tolerate systems which casually or unexpectedly violate known business rules. That leads to angry consumers, junk data, broken workflows, and lawsuits.

3. When our product can capture and enforce those rules with confidence, that's both an important differentiator and also a kind of moat/stickiness.

4. Therefore there is a strategic business justification for Engineering to fence-off where we use LLMs in production. When we use them for design, it's to create better deterministic systems than before.

children.text:
The problem will remain due to information theoretic concerns. It is not possible for an AI to read minds. You can say to an AI "build me an accounting system for a small tax firm" and we can, for the sake of argument, even stipulate that it will produce a functional system based strictly off that prompt. However, no matter how smart the AI, the result can not be any more detailed than that. Did you want it for MacOS? It may have built it for windows. Did you want it integrated into an already-existing database server? It can't have done that, and since you didn't specify the database you want it could have guessed wrong, and certainly can't guess about what tables you may already have you want to integrate into. It probably didn't guess your jurisdiction correctly (unless it was fed that in some other contextual prompt). It can't guess your most common work flows and optimize them. It can't pick out specialized features you want just for your special use case.

None of that is because AIs aren't good. It's just plain information.

An AI could sit there and interrogate the user for this information. In that alone, it would already have exceeded what a lot of people are going to want from a system like this. People, normal people, want AIs to magic stuff into existence, not spend hours interrogating them for a design requirements elicitation. That's a barrier a lot of people will not cross, and the AI companies, who fully realize that, aren't building that way.

Normal people do not want to even do the work it takes to fully specify a problem, even if an AI walks them right through it, let alone the verification that the work is correct, and actually what they intended rather than what they asked for.

And of course, in practice, AIs are not emitting bug-free code, miss entire requirements at a shot, and have a variety of other characteristic failure modes in this space that I expect are fundamental to the LLM architecture and aren't ever going to leave. If they continue to be able to make bigger systems they will simply continue to make correspondingly big errors and omissions in the process. No comment as to what the next generation AI architecture will do, though.

But, will that problem remain or is it simply that the models haven't been RLVRd on QA tasks yet? QA feels like a very RL suitable problem. You can take a codebase that has a known set of bugs in it, and proceed to train the model until it identifies those bugs. You can even generate such programs automatically by having adversarial training going on (one model deliberately writes a buggy program, another searches for the bugs). This works even with GUI bugs, drifts from the specs and so on.

I don't see any theoretical reason that this weakness must remain for longer than six months or so. I mean, both Claude and GPT are very good at doing code reviews and that's a form of QA.

children.author: mike_hearn
children.text: A lot of this is downstream of C not having a proper widely accepted unit test framework. There's no JUnit equivalent for C, in terms of sheer hegemonic adoption, nor any of the techniques that were developed to make code testable (DI, mocking libs, etc).

I have a unique perspective on this as I've been working on rewriting and rearchitecting Postgres to solve a lot of the long standing issues Postgres has[0][1].

If I had to root cause why we're finding so many bugs now, I would attribute it to the limited Postgres test suite. AI is merely uncovering bugs that already existed. For the most part, Postgres relies on individual regression tests to test each feature. While regression tests are great for making sure features don't break (yes, SELECT 'Hello, World' LIKE '%Hello%' still returns true), they actually aren't that great hitting the edge cases (passing a string that's over 2MB to a specific function will trigger a buffer overflow and crash your DB). The main way Postgres has prevented bugs in the past has been by minimizing risky changes and having lots of human review. As we're learning now, there were lots of gaps that were not caught by the existing process.

While the Postgres team is skeptical of AI, I've had lots of success in using AI to scale more advanced forms of testing such as Deterministic Simulation Testing, differential coverage guided fuzzing, and formal verification. To put it in perspective, in the process of doing testing for pgrust, I've uncovered ~50 different bugs in core Postgres. The bugs I'm finding aren't through AI review, but are instead through using AI to do more advanced testing than regression testing. All of the techniques I'm using existed existed pre-AI, but aren't used in meaningful capacity as part of the core Postgres development.

Right now I'm going all in on formal verification. I wrote a compiler to translate C and Rust functions to Lean and am then having an LLM write a proof that the two functions are identical. So far I've been able to verify 10.5% of the codebases behave identically (10.5% = 67k/640k LOC of Postgres). I'm finding details as minute as a parsing function where Postgres trimmed spaces using isspace() and pgrust only trimmed ascii whitespaces. These aren't cases you would find with traditional regression testing or human review. The thoroughness of the types of bugs I'm finding is giving me confidence that that this is catching more bugs than any sort of manual testing could. I don't currently see any reason that I won't be able to scale up the formal verification to cover 100% of the codebase. The only issue is it takes a long time to do.

children.text:
What makes you think that the number of bugs is finite? 
There are alternatives to that possibility. A perfect program without bugs might be like a perfect definition of the concept of "chair". Whatever definition you come up with there will likely be edges cases that makes the definition awkward or incorrect, and any definition that takes into account all those cases will not be a particularly good or useful definition.

> There are always more bugs to be found

A common misunderstanding.

The # of bugs lurking in a codebase is finite. At some point, the only way to find more is introduce fresh bugs through new code.

What we're seeing now is a transition phase where pre-existing bugs are found (and hopefully fixed) at an increased rate.
